## Unpaid debt or non-payment for services

**Intended claim type:** `sc-claim-unpaid-debt-services` (Unpaid debt or non-payment for services)

### FABRICATED TEST STORY -- not a real case, constructed for this survey only

> I run a small graphic design business. I signed a services agreement with a local bakery, Maple & Crumb, to design their full brand identity for a fee of $6,200, due within 15 days of delivery. I delivered all the final files on time and they confirmed receiving everything by email. This is an unpaid invoice -- Maple & Crumb never paid me anything, even after two written demand emails asking for payment.

- [FABRICATED TEST DOCUMENT] Demand email dated three weeks after delivery, asking for payment.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

```
DRAFT STATEMENT OF CLAIM -- PROPOSAL ONLY, NOT A FINAL DOCUMENT

This draft was assembled from the facts you provided during intake. It is a starting point for you to review, correct, and complete -- CourtSimplified has not verified these facts, has not decided whether this claim is appropriate to file, and this is not ready to file as written. Replace every bracketed placeholder, check every paragraph against what actually happened, and have the final version reviewed before it is used.

PARTIES
1. The Plaintiff is [Plaintiff name to be confirmed], of [Plaintiff address to be confirmed].
2. The Defendant is [Defendant name to be confirmed], of [Defendant address to be confirmed].

NATURE OF THE CLAIM
3. This is a claim for unpaid debt or non-payment for services.

FACTS (in the Plaintiff's own words, as provided during intake)
4. About six weeks ago.
5. I run a small graphic design business.
6. I signed a services agreement with a local bakery, Maple & Crumb, to design their full brand identity for a fee of $6,200, due within 15 days of delivery.
7. I delivered all the final files on time and they confirmed receiving everything by email.
8. This is an unpaid invoice -- Maple & Crumb never paid me anything, even after two written demand emails asking for payment.

AMOUNT CLAIMED
9. The Plaintiff claims $6,200 from the Defendant.
10. I want the court to order Maple & Crumb to pay the full $6,200 owed.

RELIEF SOUGHT
(a) payment of $6,200;
(b) interest and costs of this proceeding, as the court may allow.

PARTICULARS STILL NEEDED BEFORE THIS COULD BE FILED:
- Plaintiff's full legal name
- Plaintiff's address for court forms
- Defendant's full legal name
- Defendant's address for service

This is a proposal for your review, not a final document. Confirm every fact above before using it.
```

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- Under the Occupiers' Liability Act, an occupier's general duty to keep premises reasonably safe does not apply to risks a person willingly assumed by entering -- though even then, the occupier still can't deliberately create a danger or act with reckless disregard for that person's safety. A signed waiver or release is often raised in connection with this. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/90o02_eV006.doc)
- Ontario's Negligence Act says that when a court finds the plaintiff's own fault or negligence contributed to their damages, the court apportions (divides) the damages between the parties in proportion to their respective degree of fault, rather than an all-or-nothing result. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/elaws_statutes_90n01_e.doc)
- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)

Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)
- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

**System 2 -- `legal_form_mapping_rules` verified-confirmation path (`/api/cases/form-applicability`):** NOT run for this survey -- that path is gated on an authenticated, saved case in Supabase (`getAuthenticatedOwnedCase`), which this in-memory pipeline run never creates. Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

**System 2 -- `legal_form_mapping_rules` verified-confirmation path (`/api/cases/form-applicability`):** NOT run for this survey -- that path is gated on an authenticated, saved case in Supabase (`getAuthenticatedOwnedCase`), which this in-memory pipeline run never creates. Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

**Intended claim type:** `sc-claim-contractor-damage` (Damage caused by a contractor's work)

### FABRICATED TEST STORY -- not a real case, constructed for this survey only

> I hired a contractor to renovate my bathroom. Partway through, the renovation went wrong -- the contractor caused water damage to the floor below by not properly sealing a pipe, and the workmanship damaged the hardwood floor in the hallway outside the bathroom too. I told them about the damage right away and gave them a chance to fix it, but they never came back.

Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)
- Ontario's Negligence Act says that when a court finds the plaintiff's own fault or negligence contributed to their damages, the court apportions (divides) the damages between the parties in proportion to their respective degree of fault, rather than an all-or-nothing result. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/elaws_statutes_90n01_e.doc)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- Ontario's Negligence Act says that when a court finds the plaintiff's own fault or negligence contributed to their damages, the court apportions (divides) the damages between the parties in proportion to their respective degree of fault, rather than an all-or-nothing result. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/elaws_statutes_90n01_e.doc)
- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)

### Forms recommended -- two separate systems, reported separately (they can disagree)

**System 1 -- deterministic, `buildAuthoritativeRequiredForms` (`AnalysisResult.requiredNextForms`, no AI, no DB):**

`notNeededNow`: ["Form 9A — Defence unless you were served with someone else's claim"]

**System 2 -- `legal_form_mapping_rules` verified-confirmation path (`/api/cases/form-applicability`):** NOT run for this survey -- that path is gated on an authenticated, saved case in Supabase (`getAuthenticatedOwnedCase`), which this in-memory pipeline run never creates. Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default. (Source: https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)

### Forms recommended -- two separate systems, reported separately (they can disagree)

**System 1 -- deterministic, `buildAuthoritativeRequiredForms` (`AnalysisResult.requiredNextForms`, no AI, no DB):**
- Form 7A — Plaintiff's Claim

`notNeededNow`: ["Form 9A — Defence unless you were served with someone else's claim"]
`completedForms`: []
`receivedForms`: []

**System 2 -- `legal_form_mapping_rules` verified-confirmation path (`/api/cases/form-applicability`):** NOT run for this survey -- that path is gated on an authenticated, saved case in Supabase (`getAuthenticatedOwnedCase`), which this in-memory pipeline run never creates. Reported as a fact instead of run: per `docs/PROCEDURAL_RULES_INVENTORY.md` §5, this system has exactly 4 small-claims rows total (ids 6/7/15/18, covering Form 7A/9A/8A/10A) and none of them are gated on claim type at all -- only on `court_area=small-claims` plus procedural stage plus explicit user-confirmed applicability answers. Which of the 4 could apply is therefore identical for every one of the 19 claim types in this survey and depends entirely on case stage, not on which claim type matched.

### commonDefences card content (claimTypeOverviewContent.ts, deterministic, no AI)


- In most cases, a claim generally cannot be started more than 2 years after it was discovered (or reasonably should have been discovered). If that window has passed, this is often raised as a reason the claim can't proceed at all, separate from whether the underlying facts are true. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued)
- A defendant can file their own claim against the plaintiff (or someone else) as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A) -- for example, if the defendant believes the plaintiff owes them money too, or that someone else should be responsible. It must generally be filed within 20 days of filing a Defence, unless the court allows it later. (Source: https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/replying-claim)
